source: OGS Map 2556, Quaternary Geology of Ontario, southern sheet (Barnett, Henry and Cowan 1991), 1:1,000,000
citation: Barnett, P.J., Henry, A.P. and Cowan, W.R. 1991. Quaternary Geology of Ontario, southern sheet; Ontario Geological Survey, Map 2556, scale 1:1,000,000.

1.title: Bedrock, Precambrian - undifferentiated igneous and metamorphic rock
1.legend: Bedrock: undifferentiated igneous and metamorphic rock, exposed at surface or covered by a discontinuous, thin layer of drift
1.description: This unit comprises undifferentiated Precambrian igneous and metamorphic rock of the Canadian Shield, including granite, gneiss, metavolcanic and metasedimentary rocks that make up the ancient crystalline basement of central and northern Ontario. It is mapped where bedrock is exposed at surface or is covered only by a discontinuous, thin layer of drift, producing rugged, rock-controlled terrain with abundant outcrop, bedrock knobs and thin, patchy soils. Such crystalline bedrock is generally of low primary permeability, with groundwater movement controlled largely by fractures and joints.
1.source: Ontario Geological Survey 1991. Geology of Ontario; Ontario Geological Survey, Special Volume 4, Parts 1 and 2.

2.title: Bedrock, Paleozoic - undifferentiated carbonate and clastic sedimentary rock
2.legend: Bedrock: undifferentiated carbonate and clastic sedimentary rock, exposed at surface or covered by a discontinuous, thin layer of drift
2.description: This unit comprises undifferentiated Paleozoic (Phanerozoic) carbonate and clastic sedimentary rock, including limestone, dolostone, shale and sandstone, deposited in ancient shallow seas and forming the flat-lying sedimentary cover overlying the Precambrian basement. In Ontario these rocks underlie much of the south (the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence lowlands) and the Hudson Bay Lowland, and the unit is mapped where they are exposed at surface or covered by a discontinuous, thin layer of drift. Carbonate units in particular may develop karst features and secondary permeability, making them locally important bedrock aquifers.
2.source: Ontario Geological Survey 1991. Geology of Ontario; Ontario Geological Survey, Special Volume 4, Parts 1 and 2.

3.title: Catfish Creek Till
3.legend: Catfish Creek Till: sandy silt to silt matrix, strongly calcareous, moderately stony to stony
3.description: Catfish Creek Till is a regionally extensive, dense, overconsolidated basal till deposited during the Nissouri Stade of the Late Wisconsinan (roughly 22,000-17,000 years BP), when coalesced ice of the Huron-Georgian Bay, Simcoe and Ontario-Erie lobes flowed generally southwestward across the region. It occurs widely across southwestern Ontario as a subsurface marker unit beneath the younger, lobe-specific tills, with its stratotype exposed in the Lake Erie shore bluffs between Bradtville and Plum Point south of London. The unit has a sandy silt to silt matrix, is strongly calcareous, and is moderately stony to stony, reflecting its coarse-textured, clast-rich subglacial origin.
3.source: Barnett, P.J. 1992. Quaternary geology of Ontario; in Geology of Ontario, Ontario Geological Survey, Special Volume 4, Part 2, p.1011-1090. (Type sections: Dreimanis & Gibbard 2005.)

4.title: Maryhill Till (Erie lobe)
4.legend: Maryhill Till (Erie lobe): silty clay to clay matrix, moderate to high matrix carbonate content, clast poor
4.description: Maryhill Till is a fine-grained glacial till deposited by the Ontario-Erie (Erie) lobe during Late Wisconsinan (Port Bruce Stade) ice fluctuations advancing from the east and southeast out of the Lake Ontario-Erie basins. It is a prominent component of the surficial deposits of the Waterloo Moraine and adjacent Kitchener-Waterloo area of southwestern Ontario, where it overlies the older Catfish Creek Till. The unit has a silty clay to clay matrix with moderate to high matrix carbonate content and is clast poor, reflecting deposition of fine-grained, glaciolacustrine-influenced sediment.
4.source: Karrow, P.F. 1974. Till stratigraphy in parts of southwestern Ontario; Geological Society of America Bulletin, v.85(5), p.761-768. (Regional detail: Karrow 1993, OGS Report 283.)

5.title: Tavistock Till (Huron-Georgian Bay lobe)
5.legend: Tavistock Till (Huron-Georgian Bay lobe): sandy silt to silt matrix, silty clay matrix in south and north, moderate to high carbonate content, clast content decreases from moderate to poor northward
5.description: Tavistock Till is a Late Wisconsinan till deposited by the Huron-Georgian Bay lobe as it readvanced southeastward from the Huron and Georgian Bay basins during the Port Bruce Stade. It is widespread across the Stratford-Tavistock-Woodstock region of southwestern Ontario, where it commonly overlies glaciolacustrine sediments and the older Catfish Creek Till. The unit generally has a sandy silt to silt matrix (grading to a silty clay matrix in the south and north) with moderate to high carbonate content, and its clast content decreases from moderate to poor northward, reflecting incorporation of increasingly fine-grained, distal basin sediment.
5.source: Karrow, P.F. 1993. Quaternary geology of the Stratford-Conestogo area; Ontario Geological Survey, Report 283. (Named in Karrow 1974, GSA Bulletin.)

6.title: Mornington Till (Huron-Georgian Bay lobe)
6.legend: Mornington Till (Huron-Georgian Bay lobe): silty clay matrix, moderate to high matrix carbonate content, clast poor
6.description: Mornington Till is a fine-grained Late Wisconsinan till deposited by the Huron-Georgian Bay lobe during the Port Bruce Stade, when ice advanced out of the Huron and Georgian Bay basins across southwestern Ontario. It is characteristically developed in the Mornington Township area of Perth County and the broader Stratford-Waterloo region, where it interfingers with other lobe tills such as the Tavistock and Maryhill units. The unit has a silty clay matrix with moderate to high matrix carbonate content and is clast poor, indicating deposition of fine-textured, glaciolacustrine-influenced glacial sediment.
6.source: Karrow, P.F. 1993. Quaternary geology of the Stratford-Conestogo area; Ontario Geological Survey, Report 283. (Named in Karrow 1974, GSA Bulletin.)

7.title: Stratford Till (Huron-Georgian Bay lobe)
7.legend: Stratford Till (Huron-Georgian Bay lobe): sandy silt matrix, strongly calcareous, moderately stony
7.description: Stratford Till is a Late Wisconsinan glacial till deposited by the Huron-Georgian Bay lobe during the Port Bruce Stade, as this ice mass advanced southeastward out of the Huron and Georgian Bay basins across southwestern Ontario. It is typically encountered in the Stratford-Perth County region and adjacent parts of Waterloo County, forming part of the interfingering sequence of till sheets between the Huron-Georgian Bay and Ontario-Erie lobes. The till has a sandy silt matrix that is strongly calcareous, reflecting the incorporation of carbonate bedrock detritus, and is moderately stony.
7.source: Karrow, P.F. 1974. Till stratigraphy in parts of southwestern Ontario; Geological Society of America Bulletin, v.85(5), p.761-768. (Regional detail: Karrow 1993, OGS Report 283.)

8.title: Wartburg Till (Huron-Georgian Bay lobe)
8.legend: Wartburg Till (Huron-Georgian Bay lobe): silty clay matrix, high carbonate content in matrix, clast poor
8.description: Wartburg Till is a fine-grained Late Wisconsinan till associated with the Huron-Georgian Bay lobe, deposited in a glaciolacustrine or ice-marginal setting during ice advance into southwestern Ontario. It is a relatively restricted unit, recognized mainly in isolated exposures in Perth County west of Stratford. The till has a silty clay matrix with high carbonate content in the matrix and is notably clast poor.
8.source: Karrow, P.F. 1993. Quaternary geology of the Stratford-Conestogo area; Ontario Geological Survey, Report 283.

9.title: Port Stanley Till (Ontario-Erie lobe)
9.legend: Port Stanley Till (Ontario-Erie lobe): silt to sandy silt matrix becoming silt to silty clay near Lake Erie, strongly calcareous, moderate to low clast content decreasing southward
9.description: Port Stanley Till is a widespread Late Wisconsinan till deposited by the Ontario-Erie (Erie) lobe during the Port Bruce Stade, as ice flowed northwestward and westward out of the Lake Ontario-Erie basins across south-central and southwestern Ontario. It is extensively developed across the till plains north of Lake Erie in the London and Middlesex-Elgin county region. Its matrix ranges from silt to sandy silt, becoming silt to silty clay near the Lake Erie shore, and it is strongly calcareous with a moderate to low clast content decreasing southward.
9.source: Barnett, P.J. 1992. Quaternary geology of Ontario; in Geology of Ontario, Ontario Geological Survey, Special Volume 4, Part 2, p.1011-1090. (Type reference: Cowan 1975.)

10.title: Elma Till (Huron-Georgian Bay lobe)
10.legend: Elma Till (Huron-Georgian Bay lobe): sandy silt to silty matrix, clayey silt along southern margin, moderately stony, strongly calcareous
10.description: Elma Till is a Late Wisconsinan glacial till laid down by the Huron-Georgian Bay lobe during the Port Bruce Stade, when ice advanced southeastward from the Huron and Georgian Bay basins into southwestern Ontario. It is typically found across the till plains of Perth, Wellington and northern Waterloo counties, interfingering with other Huron-Georgian Bay and Erie lobe tills. The unit has a sandy silt to silty matrix, grading to clayey silt along its southern margin, and is moderately stony and strongly calcareous owing to abundant carbonate-derived detritus.
10.source: Karrow, P.F. 1974. Till stratigraphy in parts of southwestern Ontario; Geological Society of America Bulletin, v.85(5), p.761-768. (Regional detail: Karrow 1993, OGS Report 283.)

11.title: Rannoch Till (Huron-Georgian Bay lobe)
11.legend: Rannoch Till (Huron-Georgian Bay lobe): silt to clayey silt matrix becoming finer grained southward, highly calcareous, clast poor
11.description: Rannoch Till is a Late Wisconsinan till deposited by the Huron-Georgian Bay lobe, which advanced southeastward out of the Lake Huron and Georgian Bay basins across southwestern Ontario. It occurs as a surface till in the interlobate region of west-central southwestern Ontario, generally between the Lake Huron shoreline and the Stratford-Woodstock area. The unit is fine-textured, with a silt to clayey silt matrix that becomes finer grained southward, is highly calcareous owing to incorporation of local Paleozoic carbonate bedrock, and is clast poor.
11.source: Barnett, P.J. 1992. Quaternary geology of Ontario; in Geology of Ontario, Ontario Geological Survey, Special Volume 4, Part 2, p.1011-1090; Barnett, Henry & Cowan 1991, OGS Map 2556.

12.title: Dunkeld Till (Huron-Georgian Bay lobe)
12.legend: Dunkeld Till (Huron-Georgian Bay lobe): silt matrix, high matrix carbonate content, clast poor
12.description: Dunkeld Till is a Late Wisconsinan till laid down by the Huron-Georgian Bay lobe as it flowed southeastward from the Huron and Georgian Bay basins. It is mapped as a surface till in western Ontario in the region adjacent to the Lake Huron shore and the Bruce lowland. The till has a silt matrix with high matrix carbonate content, reflecting reworking of the underlying Paleozoic limestone and dolostone bedrock, and it is clast poor.
12.source: Barnett, P.J. 1992. Quaternary geology of Ontario; in Geology of Ontario, Ontario Geological Survey, Special Volume 4, Part 2, p.1011-1090; Barnett, Henry & Cowan 1991, OGS Map 2556.

13.title: Newmarket Till (Simcoe lobe)
13.legend: Newmarket Till (Simcoe lobe): sandy silt to silt matrix, moderate to high in matrix carbonate content, clast content moderate to high
13.description: Newmarket Till is the regionally extensive Late Wisconsinan subglacial (lodgement) till deposited by the Simcoe lobe in the Lake Simcoe basin and across the Greater Toronto Area, where it forms a widespread drumlinized till plain and underlies the Oak Ridges Moraine as a regional aquitard. It has a sandy silt to silt matrix with moderate to high matrix carbonate content and a moderate to high clast content, consistent with a dense, overconsolidated basal till. The unit is a key stratigraphic marker in the south-central Ontario succession and is commonly incised by north-south tunnel channels beneath the moraine.
13.source: Barnett, P.J., Sharpe, D.R., Russell, H.A.J., Brennand, T.A., Gorrell, G., Kenny, F. and Pugin, A. 1998. On the origin of the Oak Ridges Moraine; Canadian Journal of Earth Sciences, v.35, p.1152-1167.

14.title: Wentworth Till (Ontario-Erie lobe)
14.legend: Wentworth Till (Ontario-Erie lobe): sandy silt to silt matrix becoming finer grained to silty clay near Lake Erie, highly calcareous, clast content moderate to low decreasing southward
14.description: Wentworth Till is a Late Wisconsinan (Port Huron/Mackinaw stade) till deposited by westward- and northwestward-moving ice of the Ontario-Erie lobe as it readvanced from the Lake Ontario and Lake Erie basins. It is the dominant surface till of the Hamilton-Guelph-Cambridge region, where it forms the Guelph drumlin field and the Paris, Galt and Moffat moraines. The till has a sandy silt to silt matrix that becomes finer grained to silty clay near Lake Erie, is highly calcareous, and has a moderate to low clast content decreasing southward, being notably bouldery and stony within the moraines.
14.source: Karrow, P.F. 1963. Pleistocene geology of the Hamilton-Galt area; Ontario Department of Mines, Geological Report 16, 68p.

15.title: St. Joseph Till (Huron-Georgian Bay lobe)
15.legend: St. Joseph Till (Huron-Georgian Bay lobe): silt to silty clay matrix, clay content increases southward, clast poor
15.description: St. Joseph Till is a fine-grained, clast-poor glacial till deposited by the Huron-Georgian Bay lobe, which advanced southeastward out of the Lake Huron basin during the Late Wisconsinan (Port Huron Stade). It occurs at surface along the southeastern shore of Lake Huron in southwestern Ontario, in the vicinity of the community of St. Joseph and Grand Bend. The unit has a silt to silty clay matrix in which clay content increases southward, and it is clast poor, reflecting deposition from fine-textured, basin-derived debris.
15.source: Barnett, P.J. 1992. Quaternary geology of Ontario; in Geology of Ontario, Ontario Geological Survey, Special Volume 4, Part 2, p.1011-1090; Barnett, Henry & Cowan 1991, OGS Map 2556.

16.title: Kettleby Till (Simcoe lobe)
16.legend: Kettleby Till (Simcoe lobe): predominantly silt to silty clay matrix, highly calcareous, clast poor
16.description: Kettleby Till is a fine-grained, clast-poor surface till deposited by the Simcoe lobe, which occupied the Lake Simcoe basin north of Toronto during the Late Wisconsinan Port Huron Stade. It is one of the uppermost stratigraphic units in the Oak Ridges Moraine region and occurs as surface till north of the moraine in the Newmarket-Kettleby area of the Greater Toronto Area. The till has a predominantly silt to silty clay matrix, is highly calcareous, and is clast poor, consistent with deposition from fine-textured, carbonate-rich glaciolacustrine and basin-derived debris.
16.source: Barnett, P.J., Sharpe, D.R., Russell, H.A.J., Brennand, T.A., Gorrell, G., Kenny, F. and Pugin, A. 1998. On the origin of the Oak Ridges Moraine; Canadian Journal of Earth Sciences, v.35, p.1152-1167.

17.title: Halton Till (Ontario-Erie lobe)
17.legend: Halton Till (Ontario-Erie lobe): predominantly silt to silty clay matrix, high in matrix carbonate content and clast poor
17.description: Halton Till is a fine-grained, clast-poor glacial till deposited by the Ontario-Erie lobe as it readvanced from the Lake Ontario and Lake Erie basins during the Late Wisconsinan Port Huron Stade (approximately 13,000 radiocarbon years BP). Formally defined by Karrow (1963) in the Hamilton-Galt area, it is the surface till across much of the western Greater Toronto Area and the Halton-Peel region and forms the Waterdown and Trafalgar moraines. The unit has a predominantly silt to silty clay matrix that is high in matrix carbonate content and notably clast poor (typically only about 1-2 percent stones), reflecting deposition from fine-textured, carbonate-rich debris reworked from underlying glaciolacustrine sediments.
17.source: Karrow, P.F. 1963. Pleistocene geology of the Hamilton-Galt area; Ontario Department of Mines, Geological Report 16, 68p. (Regional context: Barnett 1992, SV4; Barnett et al. 1998.)

18.title: Till, undifferentiated (sand to silt matrix, clast-rich, low carbonate)
18.legend: Till: undifferentiated, predominantly sand to silty to silt matrix, commonly rich in clasts, often low in matrix carbonate content
18.description: This unit comprises glacial till deposited directly by grounded ice of the Laurentide Ice Sheet, laid down as basal (lodgement and melt-out) and subordinate ablation till during the last glaciation. Its predominantly sand to silty to silt matrix, common abundance of clasts, and generally low matrix carbonate content reflect derivation largely from the erosion of Precambrian crystalline (Shield) bedrock, so it is most extensive across northern and central Ontario. Such till typically forms ground moraine and till plains of low to moderate relief, with locally drumlinized or hummocky surfaces.
18.source: Barnett, P.J. 1992. Quaternary geology of Ontario; in Geology of Ontario, Ontario Geological Survey, Special Volume 4, Part 2, p.1011-1090.

19.title: Till, undifferentiated (sandy silt to silt matrix, clast-rich, high carbonate)
19.legend: Till: undifferentiated, predominantly sandy silt to silt matrix, commonly rich in clasts, often high in total matrix carbonate content
19.description: This unit is glacial till deposited beneath and at the margin of Laurentide ice, dominated by subglacial basal till with lesser ablation material. Its predominantly sandy silt to silt matrix, common abundance of clasts, and characteristically high total matrix carbonate content indicate a provenance that includes Paleozoic carbonate (limestone and dolostone) bedrock incorporated and comminuted during ice transport. It forms extensive ground moraine and till plains, typically where ice traversed carbonate terrain along the Shield-Paleozoic contact and adjacent lowlands.
19.source: Barnett, P.J. 1992. Quaternary geology of Ontario; in Geology of Ontario, Ontario Geological Survey, Special Volume 4, Part 2, p.1011-1090.

20.title: Till, undifferentiated (sand matrix, extremely stony/bouldery, high carbonate)
20.legend: Till: undifferentiated, predominantly sand matrix, extremely stony, bouldery and high in total matrix carbonate, often associated with stratified sediments
20.description: This unit consists of glacial till deposited by Laurentide ice, distinguished by a predominantly sand matrix that is extremely stony and bouldery and high in total matrix carbonate, and it is often associated with stratified glaciofluvial sediments. The coarse, clast-rich and locally waterlaid character suggests deposition under conditions of active ice ablation and abundant meltwater, incorporating both crystalline clasts and comminuted carbonate. Such stony, sandy tills form bouldery ground moraine and hummocky ice-contact terrain and occur in parts of central and northern Ontario near the Shield-Paleozoic margin.
20.source: Barnett, P.J. 1992. Quaternary geology of Ontario; in Geology of Ontario, Ontario Geological Survey, Special Volume 4, Part 2, p.1011-1090.

21.title: Till, undifferentiated (fine-grained, silty clay to silt matrix, clast-poor, high carbonate)
21.legend: Till: undifferentiated, fine grained, predominantly silty clay to silt matrix, commonly clast poor, high matrix carbonate content
21.description: This unit is a fine-grained glacial till with a predominantly silty clay to silt matrix that is commonly clast poor and high in matrix carbonate content, consistent with a clay-rich till deposited beneath or in front of ice moving across fine-textured, carbonate-bearing substrates. Its fine texture and low stone content reflect derivation from soft shale and glaciolacustrine-clay substrates and possible subglacial deformation of previously waterlaid fines. Such clayey tills form subdued till plains and are typical of lowland areas of southern and eastern Ontario underlain by Paleozoic carbonate and shale bedrock.
21.source: Barnett, P.J. 1992. Quaternary geology of Ontario; in Geology of Ontario, Ontario Geological Survey, Special Volume 4, Part 2, p.1011-1090.

22.title: Glaciofluvial ice-contact deposits
22.legend: Glaciofluvial ice-contact deposits: gravel and sand minor till includes esker, kame, end moraine, ice-marginal delta and subaqueous fan deposits
22.description: This unit comprises stratified gravel and sand, with minor till, deposited by meltwater in direct contact with or immediately adjacent to glacier ice, so the sediments are typically poorly sorted, cross-bedded and marked by collapse structures formed as supporting ice melted. It includes esker, kame, end moraine, ice-marginal delta and subaqueous fan deposits built where meltwater debouched into standing water. In Ontario these deposits are widespread across the Shield and along former ice margins, forming prominent ridges, mounds and hummocky ice-contact topography that are important aggregate sources.
22.source: Barnett, P.J. 1992. Quaternary geology of Ontario; in Geology of Ontario, Ontario Geological Survey, Special Volume 4, Part 2, p.1011-1090; Chapman, L.J. and Putnam, D.F. 1984. The Physiography of Southern Ontario, 3rd ed.; OGS Special Volume 2.

23.title: Glaciofluvial outwash deposits
23.legend: Glaciofluvial outwash deposits: gravel and sand includes proglacial river and deltaic deposits
23.description: This unit consists of gravel and sand deposited by meltwater streams beyond the glacier margin, including proglacial river (outwash) and deltaic deposits that are generally better sorted and more clearly bedded than ice-contact deposits because they were transported and reworked away from the ice. It forms outwash plains, valley trains, spillway fills and deltas graded to former glacial-lake or river levels. In Ontario such deposits are common along meltwater spillways and outwash tracts throughout the province and are widely exploited as sand and gravel aggregate.
23.source: Barnett, P.J. 1992. Quaternary geology of Ontario; in Geology of Ontario, Ontario Geological Survey, Special Volume 4, Part 2, p.1011-1090; Chapman, L.J. and Putnam, D.F. 1984. The Physiography of Southern Ontario, 3rd ed.; OGS Special Volume 2.

24.title: Glaciolacustrine deposits (silt and clay)
24.legend: Glaciolacustrine deposits: silt and clay, basin and quiet water deposits
24.description: This unit comprises silt and clay deposited as basin and quiet-water sediments in the extensive proglacial (glacial) lakes that occupied much of the region during deglaciation, such as glacial Lakes Algonquin, Iroquois, Peel and Warren. The fine sediment settled from suspension in deep, low-energy glaciolacustrine conditions, forming flat-lying, commonly rhythmically laminated (varved) silt and clay plains. These deposits are typically fine-textured, poorly drained and of low permeability, and are widespread across southern and central Ontario. (Note: the OGS Legend_GOO_Quat sheet labels units 24-25 'glaciomarine'; the seamless Quaternary Geology of Ontario data used for mapping labels them 'glaciolacustrine' - the latter is followed here.)
24.source: Barnett, P.J. 1992. Quaternary geology of Ontario; in Geology of Ontario, Ontario Geological Survey, Special Volume 4, Part 2, p.1011-1090.

25.title: Glaciolacustrine deposits (sand, gravelly sand and gravel)
25.legend: Glaciolacustrine deposits: sand, gravelly sand and gravel nearshore and beach deposits
25.description: This unit consists of sand, gravelly sand and gravel deposited in the nearshore, beach and deltaic environments of proglacial (glacial) lakes during deglaciation. Reworked by wave and current action along former glacial-lake shorelines, it forms beaches, bars, spits and deltas that mark former lake levels. These coarser sediments are generally well-drained and more permeable than the associated glaciolacustrine basin silts and clays.
25.source: Barnett, P.J. 1992. Quaternary geology of Ontario; in Geology of Ontario, Ontario Geological Survey, Special Volume 4, Part 2, p.1011-1090.

26.title: Glaciomarine and marine deposits (silt and clay)
26.legend: Glaciomarine and marine deposits: silt and clay basin and quiet water deposits
26.description: This unit comprises silt and clay laid down as basin and quiet water deposits by settling from suspension in the deep, low-energy basins of the Champlain Sea, which flooded the isostatically depressed Ottawa and St. Lawrence Lowlands of eastern Ontario following retreat of the Laurentide Ice Sheet (roughly 13,000-10,000 years BP). The material typically forms extensive, flat to gently undulating clay plains of massive to rhythmically laminated ('Leda' or Champlain Sea) clay, often overlying glaciolacustrine muds. These deposits are of significant geotechnical and environmental note because they are commonly soft, low-permeability and locally 'sensitive' (quick) clays prone to landsliding and settlement.
26.source: Barnett, P.J. 1992. Quaternary geology of Ontario; in Geology of Ontario, Ontario Geological Survey, Special Volume 4, Part 2, p.1011-1090.

27.title: Glaciomarine and marine deposits (sand, gravelly sand and gravel)
27.legend: Glaciomarine and marine deposits: sand, gravelly sand and gravel nearshore and beach deposits
27.description: This unit consists of sand, gravelly sand and gravel deposited in the nearshore and beach environments of the Champlain Sea in eastern Ontario, where wave action and shoreline processes winnowed and reworked glacial and glaciofluvial sediment. It occurs as beach ridges, bars, spits and deltas, commonly marking former marine shorelines and the marine limit along the flanks of the Ottawa-St. Lawrence Lowlands. Being relatively coarse and well-sorted, these deposits are generally more permeable than the associated basin clays and can form local granular aquifers.
27.source: Barnett, P.J. 1992. Quaternary geology of Ontario; in Geology of Ontario, Ontario Geological Survey, Special Volume 4, Part 2, p.1011-1090.

28.title: Fluvial deposits, Pleistocene (abandoned flood plains, terrace remnants)
28.legend: Fluvial deposits: gravel, sand, silt and clay deposited on abandoned flood plains, terrace remnants
28.description: This unit comprises gravel, sand, silt and clay deposited on abandoned flood plains and terrace remnants by late-glacial and postglacial rivers and meltwater streams whose channels have since been abandoned as base levels fell and drainage networks adjusted. It characteristically forms terrace remnants perched above modern valley floors and dissected outwash surfaces, recording former higher-stage fluvial activity across Ontario. Textures range from coarse channel gravels to finer overbank silts and clays, so their permeability and engineering behaviour vary accordingly.
28.source: Barnett, P.J. 1992. Quaternary geology of Ontario; in Geology of Ontario, Ontario Geological Survey, Special Volume 4, Part 2, p.1011-1090.

29.title: Lacustrine deposits, Recent (silt and clay)
29.legend: Lacustrine deposits: silt and clay basin or quiet water deposits
29.description: This unit comprises silt and clay deposited as basin or quiet water deposits by settling from suspension in the deep, low-energy basins of modern and postglacial (Holocene) lakes, in contrast to the older glaciolacustrine plains formed in proglacial lakes. It typically forms flat-lying, fine-grained lake-bottom sediments in present-day lake basins and low-lying, poorly drained flats. As fine-grained, low-permeability, often soft and compressible material, it is of note for foundation settlement and for limiting vertical groundwater movement.
29.source: Barnett, P.J. 1992. Quaternary geology of Ontario; in Geology of Ontario, Ontario Geological Survey, Special Volume 4, Part 2, p.1011-1090.

30.title: Lacustrine deposits, Recent (sand, gravelly sand and gravel)
30.legend: Lacustrine deposits: sand, gravelly sand and gravel nearshore and beach deposits
30.description: This unit consists of sand, gravelly sand and gravel formed in the nearshore and beach zones of modern and postglacial (Holocene) lakes, where wave and current action sorted and reworked available sediment along shorelines. It occurs as beaches, bars, spits and shoreline ridges bordering present-day lake basins. Its relatively coarse, well-sorted texture makes it comparatively permeable and locally capable of storing and transmitting groundwater.
30.source: Chapman, L.J. and Putnam, D.F. 1984. The Physiography of Southern Ontario, 3rd edition; Ontario Geological Survey, Special Volume 2, 270p.

31.title: Fluvial deposits, Recent (modern flood plains)
31.legend: Fluvial deposits: gravel, sand, silt and clay deposited on modern flood plains
31.description: This unit consists of gravel, sand, silt and clay deposited on modern flood plains by present-day rivers and streams through channel migration and overbank flooding. It forms modern alluvial flats and floodplain surfaces bordering current watercourses throughout Ontario, and is typically among the youngest (Holocene to actively accumulating) surficial materials. Because it is commonly loose, saturated, heterogeneous and subject to flooding, it warrants attention for its variable permeability, low bearing capacity and hydrological connectivity to surface water.
31.source: Barnett, P.J. 1992. Quaternary geology of Ontario; in Geology of Ontario, Ontario Geological Survey, Special Volume 4, Part 2, p.1011-1090.

32.title: Organic deposits (peat, muck and marl)
32.legend: Organic deposits: peat, muck and marl
32.description: This unit consists of peat, muck and marl that accumulate in poorly drained wetlands, bogs, fens, swamps and infilled lake basins where waterlogged, anaerobic conditions retard the decomposition of plant material, and where marl (calcium carbonate) may precipitate in calcareous settings. It forms flat, wet organic terrain that is widespread in low-lying areas across Ontario, from small southern wetlands to the extensive peatlands of the Hudson Bay Lowland. Such organic soils are of considerable geotechnical and environmental concern because they are highly compressible, weak, water-saturated and generally unsuitable as foundation material without treatment.
32.source: Barnett, P.J. 1992. Quaternary geology of Ontario; in Geology of Ontario, Ontario Geological Survey, Special Volume 4, Part 2, p.1011-1090. (See also Chapman & Putnam 1984, OGS SV2.)

33.title: Lake / open water
33.description: Map unit 33 denotes open water - lakes and other permanent waterbodies shown on the Quaternary geology map - rather than a surficial geological deposit.
33.source: Ontario Geological Survey, Quaternary Geology of Ontario (seamless data set).
